comments.text:
you express near the end that it seems kind of a wild concept that we could think similar to how a diffusion model does. But I don't find this all that wild. I think that is in fact largely how we do think. Before you start speaking any sentence, you usually know the whole message you intend to convey. Whole sentences of thought occur to us and coalesce as we speak. Even whole paragraphs of ideas. The specific words aren't all there, but we can definitely conceptualize way more than one word at a time! And quite a few of us are prone to revisiting what we already said, correcting ourselves, and then trying to proceed with the rest of the thought. 
It's the form of linear communication of ideas that makes it seem like we are one-word-at-a-time thinkers, but I really believe our thoughts relate much more to the diffusion process.

comments.author: @MuhsinunChowdhury
comments.text:
19:55 I disagree. Oftentimes when I code, what I do is I'll start filling in some parts of the code at the beginning or end or at the middle that I can think of, but then as I write more and more stuff, I'll realize I need to write some more stuff based on what I previously wrote, and I'll jump around the code and basically fill in a few words here, a few lines there, rename some variables, add some methods, add some type hints, etc as I move around the chunk of code. When I'm coming up with something new, I almost never write one word and then another and then another. If I'm just writing something from memory, then yeah, I can write it word after word after word, but if I'm coming up with a solution to something without having the full solution in mind yet, then I do jump around the code a lot.

So in reality I kind of use both methods when I'm coding. Using this jumping around method helps me a lot to solve problems because I'll write down what I can think of right now, and then as I start writing things out and I notice things like bugs and I start reading through the logic to try and follow along with it, I notice potential pitfalls and potential issues and I can address them before I "commit" that code.

comments.author: @vidskipperai
comments.text:
:yt: :stopwatch-blue-hand-timer: TIMESTAMPS & Summary (by VidSkipper AI ): Gemini Diffusion is a new Google model that generates text and code incredibly fast using a different approach than traditional language models, offering rapid responses and coherent text, though it's still in early stages of development.
0:00 🚀 Gemini Diffusion Overview
• Gemini Diffusion is a new Google model capable of creating seven different apps in about 30 seconds.
• It is faster, spitting out 1300 tokens in just over a second, and can write all the Harry Potter books in about 22 minutes.
• The model uses suggested prompts for users such as creating a simulation of fireflies that move within a confined box.
2:14 🤖 Diffusion Models Explained
• Auto regressive models predict the next word based on previous words in sequence, which can be slower.
• Diffusion models are trained by adding noise to images until they become random dots, then reversing the process to recreate the image.
• Unlike sequential token prediction, diffusion models work on the entire image at once, allowing for parallel processing and faster results.
6:12 🧪 Gemini Diffusion in Action
• Gemini Diffusion is an experimental text diffusion model that users can join the waitlist for.
• The model offers rapid response, coherent text by generating entire blocks of tokens at once, and iterative refinement to correct errors during generation.
• Benchmarks show the model is very similar to Gemini 2.0 Flash Light and can create simple video game animations coded in HTML quickly.
11:13 🌐 Translation and Coding Capabilities
• Gemini Diffusion can translate text into multiple languages rapidly, processing thousands of tokens per second.
• The model is not intended to replace current large language models for coding, but rather augment them.
• Google is testing and improving Grock 3.5 and 4 to improve coding capabilities for the next version.
13:35 🤔 Understanding How Diffusion Models Work
• Diffusion models can produce realistic images even when trained only on 2D images without explicit depth information.
• These models seem to develop an understanding of depth, light, and shadows, creating coherent 3D scenes from 2D inputs.
• Researchers are exploring how these models learn and whether they develop an underlying model of objects and their positions.
16:14 🔬 Probing the Inner Workings
• Researchers used a probe to examine the inner workings of a diffusion model during image creation.
• The model demonstrates depth from internal representation early in the denoising process, even without explicit depth data.
• The model also identifies salient objects early on, indicating an understanding of the main subject in the image.
17:56 🧠 Do AI Models Understand the World?
• Andrew Ang and Jeffrey Hinton suggest AI models may understand the world by developing mental models to predict outcomes.
• These models create internal representations of the 3D world, shadows, and light, even from 2D images.
• Understanding in AI could be defined as having a mental model that predicts world outcomes, even if it differs from human understanding.
